A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MASS and provide readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated discussion and renumbered appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-pretraining experiments with TinyLlama-1.1B and Mistral-7B, alongside selection-ratio studies and graph and similarity ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline results, computational-cost measurements, and descriptive graph statistics.

M1.justification: Skill extraction, similarity-based skill merging, graph weighting, maximum reference-example similarity, aggregation, and top-ranked selection remain unchanged. The proposed taxonomy filtering appears only as future work.

E1.justification: Both versions use NuminaMath as reference data, OpenWebMath, OpenWebMath-pro, and Jiuzhang3.0 as training corpora, and the same nine evaluation benchmarks. Coding, biomedicine, and creative writing are discussed prospectively, without new evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds BM25 and DSIR to the Mistral-7B/OpenWebMath-pro comparison, which previously contained only unselected-data training and MASS. BM25 is newly evaluated in the paper; DSIR was already evaluated with TinyLlama. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 3.3.1 adds stage-wise computational-cost evaluation in A100 GPU-hours and CPU-hours. The retained benchmark evaluations keep their model sizes, token budgets, Table 1 hyperparameters, and few-shot chain-of-thought setup; the new timing assessment does not establish changes to those settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis of preprocessing overhead relative to training cost and a descriptive characterization of graph topology in Appendix B.2. Existing selection-ratio studies, graph-component and similarity ablations, score distributions, and appendix case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table 6's new degree standard deviation describes variation among graph nodes, rather than uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds BM25 and DSIR averages of 56.6% and 57.5%, respectively, for Mistral-7B/OpenWebMath-pro; MASS remains at 62.0%. Existing benchmark and ablation scores are retained, while Tables 3 and 6 add timings and graph measurements. DSIR's listed scores average about 57.3%, and Table 6's 1,230,497 edges differ from the retained Section 2.2 count of 1,184,007 without an explicit counting explanation.

T1.justification: The mathematical graph definitions, scoring equations, decomposition in Section 2.4, and alternative similarity formulas are retained. No theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption is added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution of skill-graph-based mathematical data selection and the same efficiency and effectiveness claims. Changes such as 'effectiveness' to 'efficacy' and revised conclusion wording do not materially alter those claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds a quality-diversity explanation for selection-ratio behavior, compute-overhead interpretation, and an assertion that MASS addresses model-specific skill gaps. The discussion moved from Appendix B to Section 5 adds possible coding/biomedical applications, difficulties with less clearly defined skills, and proposed taxonomy checks. Existing diversity and skill-difficulty limitations remain.

D1.justification: Table 3 newly discloses A100 usage and approximate costs: 24 GPU-hours for extraction, 0.5 for embedding, 4 for selection, 960 for training, and 2 CPU-hours for graph construction. These are resource disclosures, not demonstrated implementation changes. Hyperparameters, extraction prompts, and the code address are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) for BM25 and Zhang et al. (2025) on diversity, and expands the contrast between skill-based selection and conventional quality filtering. Section 4 and Appendix A otherwise retain their research positioning; bibliographic updates do not represent different cited works.

P1.justification: v2 moves and expands the future-work discussion into Section 5, numbers the analysis subsections, reorganizes appendix headings, lightly rewrites the conclusion, and adds an Impact Statement and conference front matter. Most existing narrative remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds computational-cost and graph-property tables and expands Table 2 with two comparator rows. Existing figures are retained, while some figures and ablation tables move or receive new table numbers within the same general layout.

improvement.justification: The added 7B comparisons and computational-cost breakdown strengthen evidence for effectiveness and efficiency, while expanded limitations clarify applicability. These provide a limited net improvement. Reporting inconsistencies temper the gain, as does the new claim of over 40% efficiency improvement against all baselines: Figure 3 still compares MASS only with unselected-data training.
